Kickapoo

Kickapoo people continue in distinct communities and governments across the United States and Mexico. This Texas-focused reading path concerns the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and selected cross-border, legal, language, education, family-policy, and planning sources; it does not represent every Kickapoo community. Several historical and ethnographic studies document particular periods and sites, while key parts of present-day community history still need direct, community-authored documentation.

Names & relationshipsKickapoo is a broad people-level directory entry spanning distinct communities and governments. This supplement focuses on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas. It does not collapse the Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, or Mexican communities into one government or imply that the Texas government represents all Kickapoo people.
A cited introduction, with more to explore.This overview draws together the linked sources below. It is an introduction, and does not replace community-authored histories or a full scholarly study.

01

Distinct communities and the Texas-focused scope

Kickapoo people are represented by distinct communities and governments in the United States and Mexico. The 1983 Texas Band of Kickapoo Act used a specific legal relationship to the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; the later Texas-hosted constitution packet’s preamble describes the Texas Tribe as organized separately and apart. The 2020 Interior Solicitor memorandum addresses a narrower federal-jurisdiction and fee-to-trust question. These records document legal wording and chronology, not every community’s own account of identity or the packet’s present consolidated legal status.

Read the sources [3] U.S. Congress [4] U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of the Solicitor [10] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas; U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs

02

Cross-border history and community participation

Two scholarly works by Elisabeth Mager Hois examine the Texas–Coahuila relationship through different publications and periods. Her 2010 chapter surveys migration and legal/economic history, drawing in part on published literature and interviews conducted in 1996–2002; the 2020 article focuses on border crossing and includes interviews from 1985–2005. Their claims are attributed to the author and periods, not counted as independent corroboration when repeated. A separate 2017 Texas intertribal public-safety report records the Texas Tribe’s participation in statewide planning; its schematic map serves the report’s planning purpose and does not define homelands. A 1867 account attributed to No-ko-aht, recorded by federal agent Franklin G. Adams and published in an edited 1932 article, offers a distinct contemporaneous perspective on a Kansas-to-Mexico journey, the Dove Creek attack, and treaty pressure. The mediation, editorial framing, and internal chronology/group-count discrepancies are explicit; this account is not treated as a verbatim or independently corroborated record. A 1875 translated diplomatic file gives the U.S. and Mexican governments’ competing positions and attached Coahuila reports during another removal effort. These are administrative perspectives, not neutral testimony; one Coahuila report states that some Kickapoo people remained at Nacimiento and other locations. The University of Texas at Austin finding aid identifies additional Latorre field notes, manuscripts, correspondence, and other collection materials relating primarily to El Nacimiento; the collection itself was not reviewed, and the archive states photography is prohibited and image publication/exhibition permission is not being granted. It is retained as a future research route, not counted as inspected primary evidence. A 2017 peer-reviewed comparison by Mager adds a Texas-focused account of land acquisition and the later economic history of the Texas Tribe, drawing on documentary research, participant observation, interviews reported from 1995–2015, and a cited 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. This is the same researcher represented by the 2010 and 2020 works; the article’s analytical thesis and interview-based claims are attributed and not treated as independent confirmation. Only the Kickapoo-focused historical passages were used; sensitive cultural descriptions were excluded.

03

What the 1983 statute and 2020 legal memorandum address

The 1983 federal act authorizes specified services, land-acquisition activity in Maverick County, and border-passage provisions. A Texas-hosted scan of the Tribe’s constitution and attached federal records documents approval of the constitution in 1989 and later amendment elections/approvals in 2017 and 2018. Its scan labels and amendment numbering are not fully consistent, and this review did not verify whether it is the current consolidated text. The 2020 Interior memorandum addresses a narrower question about federal jurisdiction in 1934 and a particular fee-to-trust application. These are dated legal records, not legal advice or proof of current implementation. The 1875 diplomatic record shows an earlier U.S.–Mexico effort to arrange removal to U.S. reservations; it records official claims and proposals, not a complete account of individual or community decisions.

04

Education and language-related programs

The Texas Tribe’s education department publicly lists a Kickapoo language program alongside other services; some initiatives on the page are explicitly labeled under development. A 2011 INALI publication provides a much deeper, dated study of the Kickapoo variety in Coahuila: phonological analysis, an ethnographic overview based on fieldwork reported for 1980–1983 and later visits, and a practical writing-system chapter that describes consultation with speakers. The book documents a specific research and orthography project; it is not a current census of language use or a description of all Kickapoo communities. The Tribe-linked Education Department publication now provides a fuller first-party account. Its Language Department says it has developed and taught curriculum since 2017, creates learning materials, and incorporates language into Head Start, tutorial and summer programs. The Head Start page lists a Kickapoo immersion-language resource book, family-engagement activities and several learning platforms. These descriptions document the department’s published approach; they do not show measured language fluency, school outcomes or current class participation. The listed immersion book and software were not inspected. The public pages also describe family, disability and other supports, without supplying the evidence needed to evaluate their delivery.

Read the sources [8] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas [12] José Luis Moctezuma Zamarrón and Fernando Nava López; Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI) [21] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas, Tribal Education Department

05

Publicly posted policy on family, culture, and community planning

A public copy of the Tribe’s Chapter 20 Indian Child Welfare Code frames child-welfare policy around protecting family and Tribal connections and preserving children’s opportunity to learn about culture and heritage. Only selected pages were reviewed; the code’s enactment date and current consolidated status remain unverified, so it is presented as a published primary policy text rather than current legal advice or evidence of outcomes. The Tribe’s June 2025 transportation safety plan records a planning process that brought together several Tribal departments and external safety partners, using TxDOT and Tribal Police data while noting limits in the latter. Among its proposed strategies are community and school outreach, including media messages that use or honor Tribal/local language, symbols, or culture. These are dated plans and proposals, not proof of implementation or a general description of Kickapoo culture. The plan’s crash data, precise locations, appendices, and web GIS were not reviewed or reproduced.

Read the sources [19] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas; prepared with Red Plains Professional [20] Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas

06

A dated housing and community-development case study

A short HUD case feature describes housing and community-development projects involving the Texas Tribe, including FEMA mobile homes during 2009–2013 and a wellness-center project. The page’s publication date is unstated, so it is useful for a limited historical case study rather than present-day program or demographic information.

Read the sources [7] U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

07

A historical synthesis and its unresolved chronology

A 2010 UNAM chapter and the 2011 INALI study trace Kickapoo histories through Great Lakes, Midwestern, Texas, and Coahuila settings, while focusing on different communities and drawing on different evidence. The chapter describes multiple migrations and the establishment of El Nacimiento; its own notes show disagreements among cited authors about the timing and victims of the 1873 El Remolino attack and about land-area figures. The 2011 study records its author’s fieldwork and ethnographic observations for specified periods. These works add valuable historical and language context but should be read alongside the relevant treaties, statutes, and distinct community sources rather than combined into a seamless migration story. The edited 1932 publication of No-ko-aht’s 1867 account also gives his perspective on the journey south and Dove Creek conflict. Its dates and numbers differ from the editor’s prefatory narrative, so the page preserves the discrepancy and does not use the account alone to settle the event chronology. A separate 1875 U.S.–Mexico diplomatic file preserves competing government arguments over attempts to move Kickapoo people from Mexico to U.S. reservations, alongside Coahuila reports that some remained at Nacimiento and other places. Because these are translated diplomatic and administrative documents written within removal negotiations, their language, numbers, and claims are attributed to the officials rather than treated as neutral or complete community testimony. Pool’s later study of Dove Creek adds a selected-page military-history reconstruction of the 1865 attack; only pages 367, 375, 379, and 385 were inspected, and its interpretation is not a community account. Mager’s 2017 comparative study adds another dated account of Texas land acquisition and economic change, based partly on interviews and a committee report, but shares an author with the 2010 and 2020 studies and does not provide independent corroboration of their repeated claims.

Constitution of the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas, with scanned amendment and federal election/approval records ↗

Publication: 1989 constitution; amendment/election papers 2017 and 2018

The Tribe-hosted 20-page scan includes the constitution and BIA election/approval papers from 1989, 2017, and 2018. The preamble describes organization as a Tribe separate and apart from the Kickapoo Tribe of Oklahoma; the 1989 approval certificate states that its approval does not authorize action contrary to federal law. Later papers document amendments to constitutional provisions. The scan’s cover wording and included amendment-number labels are not fully consistent, and it is not independently verified here as the currently operative consolidated constitution. It is a primary historical/governance record, not legal advice or a source for private enrollment details.

Historia de la tribu kikapú y de su problemática ↗

Publication: 2010; chapter pages 101–113

This 2010 Spanish-language book chapter surveys Kickapoo histories from the Great Lakes to Coahuila and Texas and discusses the formation of the Texas community, cross-border relations, land, federal recognition, and the Lucky Eagle casino context. It is a scholarly synthesis by one author drawing on earlier publications and field interviews with Kickapoo and Múzquiz residents (1996–2002); its interpretations are not a community-authored consensus. The chapter itself notes contradictory dates and figures in cited works, including the 1873 El Remolino attack and land-area totals. Read those passages as attributed historical claims rather than settled facts. The repository lists open access and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; only a link is reproduced here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full 13-page chapter read (printed pages 101–113), including historical narrative, El Nacimiento and Texas sections, source notes, and references.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Access note: Open-access PDF through UNAM repository; Spanish language; repository metadata lists CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Publication: 2011

A substantial Spanish-language study combines a short ethnographic overview of the El Nacimiento community with two phonological analyses of the Coahuila variety and a chapter on a practical writing system. The author reports six months of fieldwork in 1980–1983 and later visits in 1988 and 2010; a later chapter describes consultation and community decision-making in developing a practical alphabet. These are dated, author-attributed observations, not a measure of present language use or a universal account of every Kickapoo community. Restricted cultural descriptions were excluded from the atlas synthesis.

Historical primary account / archival publicationGeorge A. Root, editor; Kansas Historical Society; account recorded by Franklin G. AdamsSource 14

No-ko-aht’s Talk: A Kickapoo Chief’s Account of a Tribal Journey from Kansas to Mexico and Return in the Sixties ↗

Publication: Interview recorded May 31, 1867; edited/published February 1932, Kansas Historical Quarterly 1(2), pp. 153–159

The article prints a May 31, 1867 account attributed to Kickapoo leader No-ko-aht and recorded in shorthand by federal agent Franklin G. Adams. No-ko-aht describes travel between Kansas and Mexico, the 1865 Dove Creek conflict, life in Coahuila, and his objections to treaty pressure and settler encroachment. This is a historically valuable but mediated account: the recorder was a federal agent, George A. Root edited and published it in 1932, and the surrounding editorial narrative uses period terminology and makes claims that should not be adopted as neutral fact. The printed account and editorial summary also differ in chronology and group counts; the discrepancy is retained rather than reconciled here.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full transcribed article and footnotes read, pp.153–159. Inspected the editor’s account and the attributed No-ko-aht statement; no independent corroboration of every event, date, casualty number, or quotation was established.

Review recorded: October 23, 2026

Access note: Public transcription hosted by Kansas Historical Society; source page states digitized with permission. Historical spellings, editorial framing, and one illegible passage are retained as source limitations.

Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1875, Volume II, Document 444 ↗

Publication: 1875

A translated diplomatic exchange and attached Coahuila state reports concerning U.S. efforts to move Kickapoo and other Indigenous people from Mexico to U.S. reservations. It records competing U.S. and Mexican government positions, and a Coahuila commissioner’s reports of negotiations, departures, and people still at Nacimiento and elsewhere. Those documents use coercive period language and reflect government interests; their stated counts and characterizations are not treated as neutral community testimony or a complete account of consent, movement, or later residence.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Full indexed document 444 read, including the U.S. minister’s dispatch, translated Mexican foreign-ministry reply, two attached Coahuila reports, and follow-up U.S. reply. The figures and claims are attributed to the specific officials; no independent corroboration of the reported counts or agreement was established.

Ethnic Consciousness in Cultural Survival: The Morongo Band of Mission Indians and the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas ↗

Publication: 2017

This peer-reviewed comparative study includes a dedicated section on the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and El Nacimiento. Mager identifies documentary research, participant observation, and interviews as methods and cites interviews conducted from 1995 to 2015, along with the Texas Tribe’s 1981–1984 Land Acquisition Committee report. Selected passages discuss land acquisition and economic history; the author’s theory of “ethnic consciousness,” causal claims, and generalizations remain her interpretation, not a community consensus. This is the same researcher represented by sources 6 and 11, so repeated claims are not independent corroboration. Cultural descriptions outside the selected historical scope were not used.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read article metadata and research-method statement (printed pp.47–48), Kickapoo-focused land and Texas economic-history passages (printed pp.61–63), and the corresponding cited notes on printed p.71. The comparative sections about Morongo and detailed ceremonial/cultural descriptions were not used. Claims are attributed to the author and the dates/interview sources stated in her notes.

This public copy of Chapter 20 states the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas’s child-welfare policy goals, including protecting family and Tribal connections and preserving children’s opportunity to learn about culture and heritage.
